message.content:
A common example of a **multinucleated** cell is a *skeletal muscle fiber* (also called a myocyte).  
These cells form from many individual precursor cells fusing together during development, creating a single elongated cell that contains dozens—or even hundreds—of nuclei distributed along its length.  

Other notable multinucleated cells include:

| Cell Type | Typical Function |
|-----------|------------------|
| Osteoclast | Bone‑resorbing giant cells formed by fusion of mononuclear precursors; each carries several nuclei. |
| Syncytiotrophoblast | Outer layer of the placenta; derived from trophoblastic cells that fuse into a multinucleate syncytium. |
| Some macrophage populations | In certain tissues, macrophages may contain two or three nuclei as part of their phagocytic activity. |

So if you’re looking for a “name” of a cell type characterized by having multiple nuclei, **skeletal muscle fiber** is perhaps the most classic example.
